label: Thin ice and cold water
summary: Falling through ice or into cold water kills mostly in the first minutes, not through hypothermia: you gasp and breathe hard for about a minute, and within about 10 minutes your hands, arms and legs stop working. Ice weakens with every thaw, and people who rush out to help can go through too.
signs: Grey ice: the grey is water in it. Clear blue ice is strongest; white, opaque or snowy ice is about half as strong
Ice that has thawed and refrozen, slush, and layered or rotten ice after sudden temperature changes
Snow on the ice: it insulates, so the ice under it grows slowly
Rivers and currents, changing water levels, and pressure ridges
Rising mist, air holes, and dark objects at the edge of or sticking out of the ice: the ice around them may be thinner
do: Test before you trust it: chop or drill a hole every few metres and measure the clear, hard ice. A chisel lets you test ahead as you walk

Red Cross minimums: 15 cm for walking or skating in a small group, 20 cm for a larger group, 25 cm for a snowmobile or ATV. Lifesaving Society: 20–30 cm (8–12 in) for a car, 30–38 cm (12–15 in) for a full-size pickup
Go with someone, keep apart while one of you tests, and stay off the ice at night
If you go through: for the first minute, just get your breathing under control. You then have about 10 minutes of useful movement, so use it to get out
Turn back the way you came. Get your arms onto the ice without pushing down, kick until you are flat, and slide out on your stomach, stabbing ice picks ahead. Then roll or crawl away; don't stand up
If you can't get out, get as much of your body onto the ice as you can and keep still: wet sleeves can freeze to the ice and hold you up

To rescue someone, stay on shore or solid ice: lie down and reach with a pole or branch, or throw a rope; tell them to kick while you pull. If they start pulling you toward the hole, let go and try again
dont: Don't run out to the hole to help: it most likely means two people in the water
Don't go out after a dog that falls through
Don't swim to keep warm; swim only to reach others or a safe place you can surely get to. Swimming loses heat, and your arms soon fail
Don't strip off in the water: air trapped in your clothes helps you float
Don't wear a life jacket or floater suit inside a closed vehicle on the ice
ppe: A foam life jacket or flotation suit, likely the most important item for surviving a fall through the ice; inflatable life jackets are not recommended in cold water
Ice picks, a rope, and a long pole or branch to test the ice and to reach with
A whistle on a cord around your neck, where you can reach it
firstAid: Get them off the ice into shelter, take off wet clothing, dry them, wrap them in dry layers and warm them slowly; see Cold for hypothermia
Handle them gently and watch their breathing
Warm, sweet drinks only if fully awake; no alcohol or caffeine
Not breathing: start CPR and keep going. People this cold who seemed dead have been revived
